overview: This file consists of two Department of State lists of papers indexing reports from 1938–1939 about Japanese censorship, opening, detention, and suspected tampering with foreign and official mail across East Asia. The indexed communications concern Taiwan, Harbin, Tianjin, Qingdao, Batavia, and Shanghai; record American and Iranian complaints or protests; and refer researchers to related decimal-file materials where the underlying telegrams, correspondence, reports, and an opened envelope were filed. The final entry broadens the subject from censorship to the detention of trans-Pacific mail after the U.S. Maritime Commission prohibited its carriage on American President Lines vessels.

subfiles.title: List of papers on mail censorship in Taiwan and Harbin
subfiles.about: An administrative index identifies two 1938 communications concerning official scrutiny of foreigners’ mail in Taiwan and American official mail at Harbin.
subfiles.summary: The first entry cites Shanghai telegram no. 1177 from Gauss, dated January 25, 1938, reporting that official censors opened and carefully read personal and official mail sent to or from foreigners in Taiwan, particularly foreign officials. The second cites China telegram no. 1546 from Lockhart, dated February 8, 1938, concerning the examination of official American mail at Harbin. Both entries direct researchers to related decimal-file documents, and the sheet also carries a reference to page 6.

subfiles.title: List of papers on Japanese interference with international mail
subfiles.about: An administrative index summarizes 1938–1939 reports and protests concerning Japanese censorship or detention of American, Iranian, and trans-Pacific mail.
subfiles.summary: Two Tianjin entries record American complaints about censored or tampered mail and assurances from Japanese consular officials that the matter would be investigated and that further complaints would be avoided. Other entries concern an Iranian protest reported by Grew, the detention of a U.S. Consulate letter at Qingdao, and an opened envelope submitted from Batavia as evidence of Japanese censorship. A final entry requests a report on mail from China detained at Shanghai after the U.S. Maritime Commission prohibited its transportation across the Pacific on American President Lines vessels, citing a November 7 New York Herald Tribune dispatch.

interest: The file is useful chiefly as a documentary map: it identifies censorship incidents whose substantive records were distributed among several other State Department decimal-file classifications. Its geographic range shows that interference with foreign mail was not confined to Japan itself but extended through Japanese-controlled or Japanese-influenced communications networks in China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. Particularly valuable leads include the physical opened envelope reported from Batavia, the Iranian diplomatic protest, Japanese consular assurances at Tianjin, and the intersection between wartime mail disruption and U.S. maritime policy at Shanghai. The differing file number on page 1 (“994.711”), the later DS-46 form imprint, and the reference to page 6 also illuminate the compilation and filing history of the archival bundle.
